title: Metabolic Bone Disease: Define the Mineral Pattern Before Calling It Osteoporosis
bottomLine: Low bone density, bone pain and fractures are not synonymous with primary osteoporosis. Evaluate calcium, phosphate, kidney function, vitamin D, PTH, alkaline phosphatase and the clinical context to distinguish osteoporosis from osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, CKD-mineral bone disorder and other secondary disease before choosing treatment.
recognize: Fragility fracture and low BMD can reflect primary osteoporosis, while bone pain, proximal weakness or abnormal calcium/phosphate/alkaline-phosphatase patterns may suggest a mineralization disorder.
CKD can produce complex PTH/phosphate/calcium abnormalities that should not be managed using a routine osteoporosis algorithm alone.
differentiate: Osteomalacia is defective mineralization and may accompany vitamin D deficiency, phosphate loss or other disorders; osteoporosis is loss of bone strength with normally mineralized bone.
Primary hyperparathyroidism, glucocorticoid excess, malabsorption, myeloma and thyroid disease are important secondary causes in the correct presentation.
assessment: Assess fracture pattern, bone pain, falls, nutrition, malabsorption, kidney disease, glucocorticoids/antiepileptics, endocrine symptoms, bariatric surgery and family history.
workup: Use calcium corrected for albumin or ionized calcium when appropriate, phosphate, creatinine/eGFR, alkaline phosphatase, TSH and selected PTH/25-OH vitamin D testing based on the differential.
Use BMD/vertebral imaging and additional hematologic/endocrine testing only when clinically indicated.
management: Treat the specific underlying mineral/endocrine disorder before or alongside fracture-prevention therapy.
Refer complex CKD-MBD, unexplained phosphate disorders, severe osteomalacia or recurrent fractures despite appropriate therapy to the relevant specialty.
medicationSafety: Antiresorptive drugs can worsen hypocalcemia when major vitamin D/calcium disturbance is uncorrected.
Renal function materially affects selection and monitoring of several bone medications.
redFlags: Advanced CKD with complex mineral disorder
Progressive proximal weakness/bone pain with marked biochemical abnormality
counselling: Explain why low bone density can have different causes and why correcting a mineral disorder may be as important as prescribing an osteoporosis drug.
followUp: Track the biochemical abnormality, fracture risk and functional recovery using disease-specific intervals rather than repeating all tests indiscriminately.
examTrap: Starting an antiresorptive drug solely because the BMD is low while ignoring severe vitamin D deficiency, phosphate loss or CKD-mineral bone disease.
oneLinePearl: Before treating the bone, decide whether the problem is bone quantity, mineralization, or systemic mineral physiology.

title: PCOS: Treat Reproductive, Metabolic, and Psychological Risk Together
bottomLine: PCOS is a reproductive-metabolic syndrome diagnosed only after appropriate exclusion of important mimics. Management should address cycle/endometrial protection, hyperandrogenic symptoms, fertility goals, cardiometabolic risk, sleep and mental health using weight-inclusive shared decision-making rather than treating the diagnosis as a cosmetic or weight problem.
recognize: Irregular ovulation, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism and polycystic ovarian morphology/AMH criteria can contribute to diagnosis under age-appropriate guideline rules.
Insulin resistance, dysglycemia, dyslipidemia, obstructive sleep apnea, depression/anxiety and infertility are common associated concerns.
differentiate: Exclude pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia and other causes when clinically indicated; rapidly progressive virilization suggests an androgen-secreting tumor rather than routine PCOS.
Adolescent diagnosis requires caution because normal pubertal irregularity/acne can mimic adult PCOS features.
assessment: Assess menstrual pattern, androgenic symptoms, fertility goals, pregnancy plans, BP, glycemic/lipid risk, sleep apnea, eating disorder symptoms, mood, medications and family cardiometabolic history.
workup: Use targeted hormone/exclusion testing and metabolic screening according to the 2023 international PCOS guideline; pelvic ultrasound is not required in every patient and has age-specific limitations.
Assess glucose status and cardiovascular risk factors longitudinally rather than relying on BMI alone.
management: Use cycle regulation/endometrial protection, antiandrogen/combined hormonal strategies where appropriate, and fertility-specific treatment when pregnancy is desired.
Use metformin primarily for metabolic/glycemic indications and selected cycle benefits; health-behaviour and weight-management interventions should focus on health outcomes without stigma.
medicationSafety: Antiandrogens require reliable pregnancy prevention because of fetal risk; combined hormonal therapy requires standard thrombotic/contraindication assessment.
Inositol evidence remains limited/variable; do not present supplements as a substitute for evidence-based metabolic or fertility care.
counselling: Explain that PCOS can affect periods, fertility, metabolism and mental health and is not caused by personal failure or body size alone.
followUp: Reassess cycle protection, metabolic risk, fertility goals and medication tolerability; repeat glucose/lipid screening according to current risk-based guidance.
examTrap: Diagnosing PCOS from an ultrasound alone or telling every patient that weight loss is the only treatment.
oneLinePearl: PCOS care is reproductive plus metabolic plus psychological care—not an ovary image and not a weight lecture.
sourceBasis: 2023 International Evidence-Based Guideline for Assessment and Management of PCOS
SOGC current PCOS-related position statements and Canadian reproductive practice

title: Lipid Disorders: Identify Genetic and Secondary Patterns, Then Treat Absolute Risk
bottomLine: Dyslipidemia management begins with the phenotype and the patient's ASCVD risk. Identify statin-indicated conditions, familial hypercholesterolemia and severe hypertriglyceridemia, investigate secondary causes when appropriate, and intensify therapy according to current Canadian risk/threshold guidance rather than chasing one LDL value in isolation.
recognize: Established ASCVD, LDL-C at or above the severe/genetic range, diabetes and CKD can create statin-indicated conditions.
Very high triglycerides can shift the immediate concern toward pancreatitis rather than long-term ASCVD risk alone.
differentiate: Familial hypercholesterolemia is suggested by severe LDL elevation plus family/personal premature ASCVD and requires family cascade consideration.
Hypothyroidism, nephrotic disease, diabetes, alcohol and medications can produce secondary lipid abnormalities.
assessment: Assess ASCVD, BP, diabetes, CKD, smoking, family premature ASCVD, pregnancy plans, alcohol, medications, diet pattern and prior statin tolerance.
workup: Use fasting or nonfasting lipids as appropriate; CCS recommends Lp(a) measurement once in a lifetime as part of initial lipid-risk assessment.
Use ApoB/non-HDL-C and secondary-cause testing when they answer the clinical question.
management: Use CCS primary- or secondary-prevention algorithms for statin therapy and nonstatin intensification.
Address severe hypertriglyceridemia, diabetes/alcohol/medication drivers and pancreatitis risk separately from LDL-focused therapy.
medicationSafety: Evaluate major statin interactions and clinically important muscle/liver symptoms without labelling every ache as permanent statin intolerance.
Pregnancy/planning pregnancy requires medication-specific review of lipid-lowering drugs.
redFlags: Marked muscle weakness/dark urine on therapy
counselling: Explain that the same lipid value can imply different treatment depending on lifetime/absolute vascular risk and family/genetic context.
followUp: Reassess lipids after therapy changes and close the loop on family screening when FH is suspected/confirmed.
examTrap: Treating an LDL result without assessing whether the patient already has ASCVD, diabetes, CKD or familial hypercholesterolemia.
oneLinePearl: Name the lipid phenotype and vascular risk before choosing the intensity of treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society Dyslipidemia Guideline 2021 and current CCS lipid resources

title: Obesity Pharmacotherapy: Choose Long-Term Treatment for Health Outcomes
bottomLine: Obesity is a chronic relapsing disease. Canadian 2025 pharmacotherapy guidance recommends selecting long-term medication according to adiposity-related complications, treatment goals, effectiveness, safety, contraindications, interactions, cost/access and patient preference—not using medication as a temporary reward for achieving a target number on the scale.
recognize: Obesity-related health effects include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, HFpEF, OSA, MASH, osteoarthritis, reproductive and functional complications.
BMI is an imperfect surrogate for adiposity-related disease; central adiposity and complications help define who may benefit from pharmacotherapy.
differentiate: Unintentional weight loss requires diagnostic evaluation and is not an obesity-treatment success.
Eating disorders, medications, endocrine disease and social barriers can alter the management plan.
assessment: Ask permission to discuss weight/adiposity; assess health complications, trajectory, eating disorder symptoms, pregnancy plans, cardiovascular/psychiatric history, medications, prior treatment, cost/access and patient-defined goals.
workup: Screen for obesity-related metabolic/mechanical complications according to risk; do not perform broad endocrine testing without a clinical indication.
management: Offer evidence-based pharmacotherapy alongside health-behaviour support when guideline eligibility and patient goals support it; the 2025 Canadian update includes semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide, naltrexone/bupropion, orlistat and selected rare-disease therapy according to indications.
Continue effective therapy long term when benefits outweigh harms because stopping commonly leads to weight regain and regression of health benefits.
medicationSafety: Match drug contraindications and adverse effects to the patient; pregnancy/planning pregnancy generally requires stopping anti-obesity pharmacotherapy and using an alternative plan.
Do not use compounded or non-approved medications as substitutes for Health Canada-approved obesity pharmacotherapy.
redFlags: Acute pancreatitis/gallbladder or severe GI symptoms where relevant to therapy
counselling: Set goals around health, function and complications rather than moralizing weight; explain that long-term medication is analogous to chronic treatment for hypertension or diabetes.
followUp: Track health outcomes, tolerability, adherence/access and patient goals; discontinue/switch when benefit is insufficient or harms outweigh benefit.
examTrap: Stopping effective obesity pharmacotherapy automatically after initial weight loss because medication is assumed to be short-term.
oneLinePearl: Obesity medication is chronic disease therapy—choose it for health benefit and plan for long-term use when effective.
sourceBasis: Obesity Canada Canadian Adult Obesity Clinical Practice Guideline — Pharmacotherapy in Obesity Management, updated 2025

title: Sodium and Potassium Disorders: Treat Neurologic and Electrical Risk Before the Number
bottomLine: Electrolyte emergencies are physiology problems. For sodium, determine tonicity, symptoms, duration and volume state and avoid unsafe overcorrection. For potassium, confirm the result when appropriate, obtain ECG/monitoring when severe, stabilize the myocardium when indicated, shift potassium transiently and remove excess potassium while correcting the cause.
recognize: Acute symptomatic hyponatremia can cause brain edema, seizure and coma; chronic hyponatremia carries major overcorrection risk.
Hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening conduction abnormalities even when typical ECG changes are incomplete or absent.
differentiate: Hyperglycemia can lower measured sodium without true hypotonic water excess; pseudohyponatremia and nonhypotonic states require a different approach.
Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis must be considered in a stable patient with discordant ECG/context, but treatment should not be delayed in a true unstable hyperkalemic emergency.
assessment: Assess neurologic status, seizure, volume status, kidney/heart/liver disease, fluid intake/loss, medications, endocrine disease and timing of sodium change.
For potassium, assess ECG, weakness/arrhythmia, renal function, acid-base status, tissue breakdown and RAAS/potassium-altering drugs.
workup: For hyponatremia use serum/urine osmolality and urine sodium with clinical volume context when needed; correct for glucose when appropriate.
Repeat potassium and obtain ECG when severe/symptomatic while investigating kidney failure, acidosis, insulin deficiency, tissue breakdown or medication causes.
management: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia requires monitored hypertonic-saline treatment with small controlled correction and frequent sodium checks according to the acute protocol; chronic/uncertain-duration disease requires strict overcorrection prevention.

Hyperkalemic emergency requires cardiac monitoring, myocardial stabilization with calcium when indicated, intracellular shift therapy and definitive potassium removal/dialysis strategy according to severity/renal function.
medicationSafety: Overly rapid chronic hyponatremia correction risks osmotic demyelination.

Insulin used for hyperkalemia can cause delayed hypoglycemia and requires glucose monitoring; RAAS blockade and potassium-sparing drugs require cause/risk review rather than automatic permanent discontinuation after every mild elevation.
counselling: Teach medication/fluid/sick-day factors relevant to the underlying cause after stabilization; avoid generic dietary restriction without identifying the mechanism.
followUp: Recheck electrolytes after treatment or medication changes at a clinically appropriate interval and close the loop on the underlying renal/endocrine cause.
examTrap: Correcting chronic hyponatremia rapidly to 'normal' or treating hyperkalemia only by shifting potassium without a plan to remove it from the body.
oneLinePearl: Sodium threatens the brain; potassium threatens the cardiac membrane—treat the physiology and the cause.
sourceBasis: Emergency Care BC Hyponatremia and Hyperkalemia clinical summaries

title: Calcium Disorders: Confirm the Active Calcium, Then Find PTH-Dependent or PTH-Independent Cause
bottomLine: Calcium abnormalities require confirmation and mechanism. Use albumin-corrected or ionized calcium when appropriate, then interpret PTH, kidney function, phosphate, magnesium, vitamin D and the clinical context. Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia or hypocalcemia is an emergency; mild chronic disease needs cause-directed evaluation before treatment.
recognize: Hypercalcemia can cause polyuria, dehydration, constipation, weakness, confusion and arrhythmia; hypocalcemia can cause paresthesias, tetany, seizure and QT prolongation.
Albumin abnormalities can make total calcium misleading; ionized calcium is useful when binding/pH changes make correction unreliable.
differentiate: High/inappropriately normal PTH with hypercalcemia suggests PTH-dependent disease; suppressed PTH shifts toward malignancy, vitamin D, medication or other PTH-independent causes.
Hypocalcemia with low/inappropriately normal PTH differs from vitamin D deficiency/CKD states with secondary PTH elevation.
assessment: Review symptoms, kidney stones, fractures, malignancy, thyroid/parathyroid surgery, kidney disease, vitamin D/calcium supplements, lithium/thiazides, bisphosphonate/denosumab use, pregnancy and magnesium.
workup: Confirm calcium and obtain PTH with renal function, phosphate, magnesium and selected vitamin D/urine-calcium/malignancy testing based on the mechanism.
Obtain ECG in significant symptomatic calcium disturbance.
management: Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia requires urgent IV volume/calcium-lowering therapy and treatment of the cause; avoid reflex aggressive fluids when heart/kidney failure requires careful reassessment.
Severe symptomatic hypocalcemia requires monitored IV calcium and correction of magnesium/underlying cause; stable chronic disease uses oral calcium/vitamin D or disease-specific therapy.
medicationSafety: Denosumab/bisphosphonates and other therapies can precipitate/worsen hypocalcemia when calcium/vitamin D or renal issues are not addressed.
Calcium therapy can cause hypercalciuria/stones; chronic replacement should not simply target high-normal serum values.
counselling: Explain that abnormal calcium is a clue to parathyroid, vitamin D, kidney, medication or malignancy physiology—not a diagnosis by itself.
followUp: Recheck calcium/magnesium/renal function after acute treatment and close the loop on PTH-dependent versus independent evaluation.
examTrap: Ordering parathyroid imaging before establishing PTH-dependent hypercalcemia or treating refractory hypocalcemia without checking magnesium.
oneLinePearl: Confirm calcium, check PTH, and treat severe neurologic/electrical symptoms before chasing the final diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Emergency Care BC electrolyte emergency principles
